newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila food complex fails to attract buyers.
newsitem.headline: Manila food complex fails to attract buyers.

text.p: The Philippines failed on Wednesday to attract buyers for a sprawling agro-industrial complex as fears of a property glut discouraged prospective bidders, officials and local executives said.

Rising domestic interest rates and stiff provisions in the privatisation terms might have also turned away prequalified bidders for the Food Terminal Inc (FTI), a senior agriculture department official told Reuters.
"Fears that the Philippine property sector might have reached its peak and may go bust any time affected the bidding," the official added.

"The projected return on investment was not commensurate to the initial investment that the bidders are required to pay," an official of Filinvest Development Corp, one of the qualified bidders, told Reuters.
"Besides, most of the FTI property has been leased," he said, adding that the winning bidder may have to wait for many years before it could fully develop the property.
Filinvest and Metro Pacific Corp sent letters informing the government they were not going to bid after reviewing the project's feasibility.

"The privatisation of Food Terminal Inc (FTI) does not conform with their corporate plans," Agriculture Assistant Secretary Marinela Castillo said when asked why qualified bidders decided to withdraw from the auction.
On Tuesday, another qualified bidder, Keppel Corp Ltd, also announced in Singapore that it was not joining the bidding.
FTI president Romeo David said interested buyers have also been deterred by a contract provision requiring a three-fourths majority vote on any major decision regarding the terminal complex.
The government was selling the 51 percent stake in a food terminal at the edge of Manila's Makati financial district for at least 6.97 billion pesos.
State agency National Food Authority will retain 35 percent of its stake and the remaining 14 percent will be offered to small local investors.
David said FTI bidders complained that the contract provisions were too stiff.
Of the 121 hectares inside the food storage complex, only 80 hectares is leasable.
"FTI has lease agreements covering 51 hectares of the property for up to 30 years" said David.
Some 500 lessees of FTI had complained that they were not consulted by the government on the sale of the complex and threatened to file civil suits to stop the privatisation.

Further, the winner of the FTI privatisation is required to maintain the existing cold storage facilities covering 11.6 hectares, including a pre-inspection area for Philippine mangoes for export to Japan.

The terminal was formed in 1968 to stabilise prices of commodities in Manila through an efficient agricultural marketing system. Deterioration of stocks and high interest costs, however, had hit the complex and resulted in huge losses.
